questions.title: Database Partitioning vs Sharding
questions.question: What is the difference between database partitioning and sharding?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Partitioning: split table within one DB (range, list, hash)**
- **Sharding: split data across multiple DB servers (scale-out)**
- **Partition pruning: queries only read relevant partitions**
- **Shard key: determines which server holds the data — choose carefully**
- **Sharding complexity: no cross-shard JOINs, distributed transactions are hard**
- **Most systems never need sharding — exhausts vertical scaling, caching first**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Partitioning splits a large table into smaller segments within the same database server. Range partitioning by date is the most common example — January data in one partition, February in another. The database can then skip irrelevant partitions when you query by date, dramatically speeding up time-range queries and making it easy to archive old data by dropping an entire partition.

Sharding takes this further by distributing data across completely separate database servers. Each server (shard) holds a subset of the data determined by the shard key — for example, user IDs 1-1M on shard 1, 1M-2M on shard 2. This provides horizontal scaling beyond what any single server can handle.

Sharding comes with serious complexity: you lose cross-shard JOINs, distributed transactions become much harder, and re-sharding as you grow is operationally painful. Most applications should exhaust vertical scaling, read replicas, caching, and partitioning before considering sharding.
